passed.title: Null and NaN are different missing values
passed.trap: pandas treats `NaN` as missing data. Polars does not: `null` is missing, while `NaN` is an ordinary float value. `Expr.is_null` returns false for `NaN`, and `Expr.fill_null` leaves `NaN` untouched. `Expr.interpolate` also leaves `NaN` in place, as its docstring example shows. To clean float columns, first convert `NaN` to null with `Expr.fill_nan(None)` and then call `Expr.fill_null`, or test for `NaN` with `Expr.is_nan`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"b": [1.0, float("nan"), None]})
out = df.select(
    pl.col("b").is_null().alias("is_null"),
    pl.col("b").is_nan().alias("is_nan"),
    pl.col("b").fill_null(0.0).alias("fill_null_only"),
    pl.col("b").fill_nan(None).fill_null(0.0).alias("nan_and_null_filled"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: NaN compares equal to NaN in Polars comparisons
passed.trap: Under IEEE/NumPy/pandas rules, every comparison with `NaN` is false. Polars treats NaNs as equal, so `Expr.ge` evaluates `NaN >= NaN` to true. `Expr.gt` gives false for that pair. A filter such as `x >= y` can therefore silently keep NaN rows. If NaN rows must not pass, exclude them explicitly with `Expr.is_not_nan`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [float("nan"), 1.0], "y": [float("nan"), 2.0]})
out = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("x").ge(pl.col("y")).alias("x_ge_y"),
    pl.col("x").gt(pl.col("y")).alias("x_gt_y"),
    (pl.col("x").ge(pl.col("y")) & pl.col("x").is_not_nan()).alias("x_ge_y_no_nan"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: is_between parses string bounds as column names and is inclusive on both ends
passed.trap: `Expr.is_between` treats string bounds as **column names**, not literals. So `pl.col("s").is_between("b", "d")` looks for columns `b` and `d` and fails. Wrap string bounds in `pl.lit` instead. The default `closed="both"` includes both endpoints, so pass `closed="left"`, `"right"` or `"none"` when you need half-open ranges such as date buckets.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"num": [1, 2, 4, 5], "s": ["a", "b", "d", "e"]})
out = df.select(
    pl.col("num").is_between(2, 4).alias("both"),
    pl.col("num").is_between(2, 4, closed="left").alias("left"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))
try:
    df.select(pl.col("s").is_between("b", "d"))
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))
ok = df.select(pl.col("s").is_between(pl.lit("b"), pl.lit("d")))
print(ok.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: Expr.flatten is deprecated since 1.38
passed.trap: `Expr.flatten` is deprecated in 1.38 and will be removed in 2.0, so do not write new code with it. The deprecation message names `Expr.list.explode(keep_nulls=False, empty_as_null=False)` as the replacement and describes it as the behaviour you likely expect. Use that form, including in `group_by().agg`, where `flatten` was commonly used to merge lists per group.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"group": ["a", "b", "b"], "values": [[1, 2], [2, 3], [4]]})
out = df.group_by("group", maintain_order=True).agg(
    pl.col("values").list.explode(keep_nulls=False, empty_as_null=False)
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: is_in propagates nulls unless nulls_equal=True
passed.trap: With the default `nulls_equal=False`, a null input to `Expr.is_in` does not produce False, and putting `None` in the lookup list does not make it match. The null propagates instead, so a filter on that mask silently drops the null rows. Pass `nulls_equal=True` to treat null as a matchable value.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, None, 3]})
out = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("a").is_in([1, None]).alias("default"),
    pl.col("a").is_in([1, None], nulls_equal=True).alias("nulls_equal"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))
print(df.filter(pl.col("a").is_in([1, None])).height)
print(df.filter(pl.col("a").is_in([1, None], nulls_equal=True)).height)

passed.title: first() returns null if the first value is null
passed.trap: pandas `groupby().first()` skips missing values. Polars `Expr.first` defaults to `ignore_nulls=False` and returns the literal first element, even when that element is null. To get the first non-null value per group, pass `ignore_nulls=True`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "a", "b"], "v": [None, 1, 2]})
out = df.group_by("g", maintain_order=True).agg(
    pl.col("v").first().alias("first"),
    pl.col("v").first(ignore_nulls=True).alias("first_non_null"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))

passed.title: is_duplicated marks every occurrence, unlike pandas duplicated
passed.trap: `Expr.is_duplicated` is true for **all** occurrences of a repeated value, including the first one. pandas `duplicated()` with keep='first' flags only the later copies. Filtering out `is_duplicated()` rows therefore drops every copy, not just the extras. `Expr.is_unique` is its exact complement. For pandas-style dedup masks, use `Expr.is_first_distinct().not_()` to keep the first copy or `Expr.is_last_distinct().not_()` to keep the last.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 1, 2, 1]})
out = df.with_columns(
    pl.col("a").is_duplicated().alias("is_duplicated"),
    pl.col("a").is_unique().alias("is_unique"),
    pl.col("a").is_first_distinct().not_().alias("dup_keep_first"),
    pl.col("a").is_last_distinct().not_().alias("dup_keep_last"),
)
print(out.to_dict(as_series=False))
passed.output: {'a': [1, 1, 2, 1], 'is_duplicated': [True, True, False, True], 'is_unique': [False, False, True, False], 'dup_keep_first': [False, True, False, True], 'dup_keep_last': [True, True, False, False]}

note.title: get raises on out-of-bounds indices unless null_on_oob=True
note.trap: `Expr.get` defaults to `null_on_oob=False`, so an index past the end raises an error instead of returning null. This bites in `group_by().agg` when some groups are shorter than others: a single short group fails the whole query. Pass `null_on_oob=True` to get null for those groups.
